Clinical implications of categories C, D and E

Category C comprises hospitalized patients who rarely benefit from therapies beyond anticoagulation; its subdivision by RV imaging and biomarkers, with lactate measurement (Class 1), is intended to identify those at risk of progression ( 9 ). Category C3, particularly with a respiratory modifier, resembles the PEITHO and HI-PEITHO populations, in whom the role of CDI is debated (Section 6.5 ) ( 31 , 32 ).

Category D is the main conceptual advance of the 2026 framework. It recognizes incipient cardiopulmonary failure in patients whose blood pressure is not persistently low: transient, fluid-responsive hypotension (D1) and normotensive shock (D2), defined by markers of hypoperfusion such as lactate >2 mmol/L, acute kidney injury, oliguria, altered mentation or a cardiac index <2.2 L/min/m 2 ( 9 ). In the FLASH registry, approximately one-third of normotensive patients with intermediate-risk PE who underwent invasive hemodynamic assessment had a cardiac index in the shock range ( 33 ), and a composite shock score combining clinical, biochemical and imaging variables has been proposed to identify them non-invasively ( 34 ). Clinically, category D implies admission to an intensive care or high-dependency unit, immediate PERT involvement, avoidance of sedation, intubation and aggressive fluid loading, early vasopressor or inotropic support, and readiness for reperfusion, for which the AHA/ACC guideline assigns a Class 2b recommendation ( 9 ). The evidence base is, however, limited: the concept derives largely from retrospective analyses of patients undergoing mechanical thrombectomy, and no prospective study has yet shown that treating normotensive shock differently improves outcomes ( 9 , 33 ).

Category E corresponds to ESC high-risk PE and mandates immediate reperfusion and circulatory support; by distinguishing refractory shock or arrest (E2), the framework specifies when VA-ECMO is reasonable and surgery without circulatory support is not preferred (Sections 6.3 and 6.6) ( 1 , 9 ). 5.5. Translating categories into monitoring and escalation

A single baseline label is insufficient because patients may progress from stable RV strain to incipient failure, a trajectory formalized by the AHA/ACC D categories ( 9 ). In the authors' opinion, the admission note of every patient at ESC intermediate-high risk or in AHA/ACC category C3–D should document explicit escalation triggers (new hypotension, rising lactate, increasing oxygen requirement, syncope, altered mentation, oliguria, progressive tachycardia or worsening RV failure), the pre-agreed rescue strategy and the responsible team, consistent with the recommendation for PERT involvement in these categories ( 1 , 9 ). 6. Acute treatment 6.1. Initial stabilization

Supportive therapy should protect RV perfusion and avoid iatrogenic collapse. Because aggressive volume loading may worsen RV dilatation and left ventricular underfilling, cautious fluid administration (≤500 mL) is reserved for patients with low central venous pressure, and norepinephrine is the first-line vasopressor for hypotension ( 1 ). Induction of anesthesia and positive-pressure ventilation can precipitate collapse by reducing venous return and increasing RV afterload; the AHA/ACC guideline therefore advises against deep sedation and intubation unless clinically necessary in patients with RV dysfunction ( 1 , 9 ). Venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) may stabilize refractory shock or cardiac arrest as a bridge to reperfusion or recovery, but it is not definitive thrombus therapy (Section 6.6 ) ( 9 , 35 ).
6.2. Anticoagulation

Anticoagulation should begin promptly, including while awaiting imaging when clinical probability is high or intermediate ( 1 ). Low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) is preferred over unfractionated heparin (UFH) for parenteral therapy in most patients because of more predictable pharmacokinetics and lower rates of recurrence without increased bleeding ( 1 , 9 ); UFH remains preferable when immediate reperfusion or another procedure is anticipated, when rapid reversal may be needed, and in severe renal impairment ( 1 ). For most eligible adults, direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) are preferred over vitamin K antagonists (VKAs). In a meta-analysis of the phase 3 trials, DOACs had similar efficacy for recurrent VTE [relative risk (RR) 0.90] and reduced major bleeding (RR 0.61), intracranial hemorrhage (RR 0.37) and fatal bleeding ( 36 – 40 ). Apixaban and rivaroxaban can be started without a parenteral lead-in, whereas dabigatran and edoxaban require at least five days of parenteral anticoagulation. In the randomized COBRRA trial, clinically relevant bleeding during three months of treatment was lower with apixaban than with rivaroxaban (3.3% vs. 7.1%; RR 0.46) ( 41 ).

Drug choice must account for renal and hepatic function, pregnancy, antiphospholipid syndrome, body weight, interactions, adherence, affordability, cancer site, thrombocytopenia and planned procedures ( Table 5 ). In cancer-associated VTE, factor Xa inhibitors were non-inferior or superior to dalteparin for recurrence, but edoxaban and rivaroxaban increased gastrointestinal and genitourinary bleeding in patients with luminal tumors, whereas apixaban did not increase major bleeding (3.8% vs. 4.0%) ( 24 , 42 – 44 ). In high-risk antiphospholipid syndrome, rivaroxaban caused an excess of thrombotic and bleeding events compared with warfarin, and VKAs remain the agents of choice ( 45 ); recommendations for obesity and pregnancy are summarized in Table 5 ( 22 , 46 ).

Systemic thrombolysis

Systemic thrombolysis is recommended for high-risk PE (ESC Class I, level of evidence B; AHA/ACC category E, Class 2a) when bleeding risk is acceptable ( 1 , 9 ). In a meta-analysis of 16 trials, thrombolysis was associated with lower all-cause mortality (odds ratio 0.53) but higher major bleeding (9.24% vs. 3.42%) and intracranial hemorrhage (1.46% vs. 0.19%) ( 47 ). In intermediate-high-risk PE, the PEITHO trial showed that full-dose tenecteplase reduced death or hemodynamic decompensation within 7 days (2.6% vs. 5.6%; odds ratio 0.44), but increased major extracranial bleeding (6.3% vs. 1.2%) and hemorrhagic stroke (2.0% vs. 0.2%), without a mortality advantage ( 32 ). Its long-term follow-up showed no benefit on survival, functional limitation or CTEPH (Section 9.2 ) ( 48 ). Accordingly, both guidelines recommend against routine systemic thrombolysis in normotensive patients (ESC Class III; AHA/ACC categories A–C2, Class 3: Harm) and favor anticoagulation with close monitoring and rescue reperfusion if deterioration occurs (ESC Class I for rescue thrombolysis) ( 1 , 9 ). For categories D1–D2, systemic thrombolysis “may be considered” (Class 2b) ( 9 ).

Reduced-dose thrombolysis is attractive: 50 mg of alteplase was as effective as 100 mg on radiological endpoints with fewer bleeding events ( 49 ), but such trials have been underpowered for clinical outcomes. The ongoing PEITHO-3 trial is randomizing approximately 650 patients with intermediate-high-risk PE and additional clinical markers of severity to reduced-dose alteplase or placebo on top of heparin, with a 30-day composite of death, hemodynamic decompensation or recurrent PE as the primary outcome ( 50 ). Contraindications should be weighed against the threat of imminent death from obstructive shock ( 1 ). 6.4. Catheter-directed intervention: terminology and evidence

For clarity, we use catheter-directed intervention (CDI) as an umbrella term for percutaneous reperfusion techniques, comprising two families ( 11 , 12 ). Local (catheter-directed) thrombolysis delivers a low total dose of fibrinolytic—typically 8–24 mg of alteplase over several hours—through standard multi-side-hole catheters (conventional catheter-directed thrombolysis, CDT) or ultrasound-facilitated catheters (USCDT). Mechanical thrombectomy (MT) removes thrombus without, or with minimal, fibrinolytic exposure, using large-bore aspiration or extraction systems or computer-assisted vacuum thrombectomy. Early evidence consisted of single-arm studies or small randomized trials with surrogate endpoints, chiefly the reduction in the RV-to-left ventricular (RV/LV) diameter ratio at 24–48 h: ULTIMA, SEATTLE II, OPTALYSE and SUNSET sPE for local thrombolysis ( 51 – 54 ), and FLARE, EXTRACT-PE and the 800-patient FLASH registry for MT ( 55 – 57 ). In high-risk PE, the non-randomized FLAME study reported in-hospital mortality of 1.9% with large-bore MT versus 29.5% in a context arm treated predominantly with systemic thrombolysis, although the groups were not comparable, so these data represent observational evidence only ( 58 ). The small CANARY trial was stopped early without a significant difference in its primary endpoint ( 59 ) ( Table 7 ).

The evidence base has changed substantially with four randomized trials ( Table 7 ). HI-PEITHO randomized 544 patients with intermediate-high-risk PE (RV/LV ≥1.0, elevated troponin) and at least two markers of physiological stress (heart rate ≥100/min, SBP ≤110 mmHg, respiratory rate ≥20/min or oxygen saturation ≤90%) to USCDT plus anticoagulation or anticoagulation alone ( 31 ). The 7-day composite of PE-related death, cardiorespiratory decompensation or collapse, or symptomatic recurrence occurred in 4.0% versus 10.3% (RR 0.39; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.20–0.77), corresponding to a number needed to treat of approximately 16. The effect was driven by cardiorespiratory decompensation (3.7% vs. 10.3%), defined to include a National Early Warning Score ≥9; PE-related death (1.1% vs. 0.4%) and 30-day all-cause mortality (1.8% vs. 1.1%) did not differ, there was no intracranial hemorrhage, and 7-day major bleeding was numerically but not significantly higher (4.1% vs. 2.2%) ( 31 ). In PEERLESS (550 patients), large-bore MT was superior to CDT on a hierarchical win ratio (5.01; 95% CI 3.68–6.97) driven by less clinical deterioration or bailout (1.8% vs. 5.4%) and lower intensive care unit (ICU) use, without differences in mortality or bleeding ( 60 ). In STORM-PE (100 patients), computer-assisted vacuum thrombectomy plus anticoagulation reduced the 48-hour RV/LV ratio more than anticoagulation alone (0.52 vs. 0.24) ( 61 ).

HI-PEITHO is thus the first adequately powered randomized trial to show that a CDI reduces early clinical deterioration. However, it was open-label and industry-funded, enrolled highly selected patients at experienced centers, relied on a composite in which a physiological score contributed substantially, and did not show reductions in mortality; long-term functional outcomes are pending ( 31 ). PEERLESS compared two interventional strategies with a resource-driven endpoint, and STORM-PE used a surrogate endpoint ( 60 , 61 ). Ongoing trials, including PEERLESS II (large-bore MT versus anticoagulation), PE-TRACT (CDI versus anticoagulation with functional endpoints) and PEITHO-3, will further define net benefit (Section 11 ).
6.5. Elective CDI in intermediate-high-risk PE with several adverse prognostic markers

Whether such patients should undergo elective CDI rather than anticoagulation with rescue therapy is the most debated question in acute PE care. Arguments in favor include the 61% relative reduction in early decompensation in HI-PEITHO ( 31 ), the low rates of intracranial hemorrhage with CDI compared with systemic thrombolysis ( 31 , 47 , 60 ), and the position statement of the Spanish Society of Cardiology, which suggests considering elective CDI within 24 h in intermediate-high-risk patients with multiple poor prognostic factors (for example, elevated lactate, syncope, borderline blood pressure or tachycardia) ( 12 ). The AHA/ACC guideline assigns a Class 2b recommendation (benefit unclear) to CDI in categories C2–C3 and “may be considered” in D1–D2 ( 9 ). Arguments for caution include the absence of a mortality benefit, the lack of long-term benefit after thrombolysis in PEITHO ( 48 ), procedural complications ( 12 , 62 ), costs, unequal access, and the fact that most patients treated with anticoagulation alone in HI-PEITHO and PEITHO did not deteriorate ( 31 , 32 ).

CDI-related complications can be grouped into access-site and vascular complications (hematoma, inadvertent arterial puncture, retroperitoneal hemorrhage, pseudoaneurysm and arteriovenous fistula); bleeding, including intracranial hemorrhage when a fibrinolytic is used; injury to the pulmonary arteries (perforation or pseudoaneurysm, presenting with hemoptysis, hemothorax or desaturation) or to the right heart (tricuspid valve damage, perforation or tamponade, and arrhythmias including atrioventricular block); periprocedural hemodynamic deterioration; and device-related problems such as catheter entrapment or kinking ( 62 ). Their reported frequency varies widely, because definitions are not standardized and reporting windows range from 48 h to 90 days ( 62 ). In the randomized trials and prospective registries summarized in a recent expert review, access-site complications occurred in approximately 1%–8% of patients, the overall rate of pulmonary artery injury was around 0.7%, and intracranial hemorrhage occurred in 0%–2% ( 62 ). Major bleeding ranged from approximately 1% with large-bore MT in the FLASH registry to approximately 7% with either MT or CDT in PEERLESS and 10% with USCDT in SEATTLE II, and it reached 11% after MT in high-risk patients in FLAME ( 54 , 55 , 58 , 60 ). Randomized trials report no or very low procedural mortality, whereas real-world data report CDI-related mortality of 3.5%–6.7%, and in the US Food and Drug Administration Manufacturer and User Facility Device Experience (MAUDE) database, pulmonary vascular perforation was the most common complication resulting in death after mechanical thrombectomy ( 62 ). Large-bore aspiration also entails blood loss, which is now mitigated by blood-return systems ( 12 ). These data support performing CDI at experienced centers, with real-time ultrasound-guided venous access, careful catheter and guidewire manipulation and predefined bail-out options such as systemic thrombolysis or surgery, and weighing the expected benefit against procedural risk in each patient ( 12 , 62 ).

Thus, the evidence supporting elective CDI consists of one randomized trial with an early clinical endpoint, surrogate-endpoint trials and registries, and expert consensus. In the authors' opinion, pending PEITHO-3, PEERLESS II and PE-TRACT, elective CDI is reasonable after PERT discussion for patients who meet HI-PEITHO-like criteria (ESC intermediate-high risk or AHA/ACC category C3 with at least two markers of physiological stress) or AHA/ACC category D1–D2, have low procedural risk and are treated at experienced centers; other normotensive patients should receive anticoagulation with monitoring and a predefined rescue strategy.
6.6. High-risk PE when systemic thrombolysis is contraindicated or has failed

For high-risk PE with a contraindication to, or failure of, systemic thrombolysis, the ESC recommends surgical embolectomy (Class I, level C) and suggests percutaneous catheter-directed treatment as an alternative (Class IIa, level C) ( 1 ); the AHA/ACC guideline considers local thrombolysis, MT and surgical embolectomy reasonable in category E1 (Class 2a) and VA-ECMO reasonable in category E2 with refractory shock (Class 2a) ( 9 ). No randomized trial has compared MT with local thrombolysis in this setting, so their relative roles rest on mechanistic reasoning, registry data and expert consensus rather than on comparative trials ( 11 , 12 , 58 ). MT provides immediate debulking without fibrinolytic exposure and is generally preferred when the contraindication is absolute (for example, recent intracranial hemorrhage or active bleeding) or when the patient cannot await a multi-hour infusion; local thrombolysis, which still exposes the patient to a low-dose fibrinolytic, may be considered when contraindications are relative, when MT is unavailable, or after incomplete mechanical debulking ( 11 , 12 ). In refractory shock or cardiac arrest, VA-ECMO can serve as a bridge to MT or surgical embolectomy; observational case series suggest better outcomes when ECMO is combined with definitive reperfusion than when it is used as stand-alone therapy, but no randomized data exist ( 9 , 35 ).
6.7. Surgical embolectomy, right-heart thrombus and PE response teams

Surgical embolectomy is an option for high-risk PE when thrombolysis is contraindicated or has failed, and for thrombus in transit or straddling a patent foramen ovale ( 1 , 9 ); outcomes depend heavily on selection and experience, with an in-hospital mortality of 27.2% in a nationwide United States cohort ( 63 ). Evidence for surgical embolectomy is limited to observational series. Management of right-heart thrombus should be individualized by a multidisciplinary team according to hemodynamic status, thrombus mobility and size, bleeding risk, patent foramen ovale and local expertise, as randomized evidence is lacking ( 1 ). The AHA/ACC guideline recommends multidisciplinary PERT evaluation for categories C–E (Class 1) ( 9 ). This recommendation rests on observational before-and-after studies: in a meta-analysis, PERT implementation increased the use of advanced therapies (RR 2.67), whereas the reduction in mortality was not significant (RR 0.89; 95% CI 0.67–1.19) ( 64 , 65 ). A PERT should therefore be judged by timeliness, appropriateness, complications and patient-centered outcomes, not by procedural volume (authors' opinion).

6.8. Inferior vena cava filters Inferior vena cava filters do not treat PE. In PREPIC2, adding a retrievable filter to anticoagulation did not reduce recurrent PE at three months (3.0% vs. 1.5%; RR 2.00) ( 66 ). Filters should be reserved for acute VTE with an absolute contraindication to anticoagulation or recurrence despite adequate anticoagulation, with a documented retrieval plan ( 1 , 9 ). 7. Transitions of care: disposition, discharge and early follow-up 7.1. Outpatient treatment and early discharge

Selected low-risk patients (ESC low risk; AHA/ACC categories A–B) can be treated at home or discharged early ( 1 , 9 ). Outpatient treatment was non-inferior to inpatient care in the randomized OTPE trial (recurrent VTE 0.6% vs. 0% at 90 days) ( 67 ); early discharge on rivaroxaban was associated with recurrent VTE or PE-related death in 0.6% in HoT-PE ( 68 ); and in HOME-PE, Hestia- and sPESI-based triage yielded similar 30-day adverse outcomes (3.8% vs. 3.6%) ( 69 ). A low clinical score is necessary but not sufficient. Oxygen requirement, bleeding risk, renal function, comorbidity, pain control, medication access, health literacy and social support must also be favorable ( 30 , 69 ). In the authors' opinion, when medication access, housing, transport, language support or follow-up are unreliable, a brief admission may be safer than nominally guideline-concordant discharge.
7.2. The minimum discharge bundle

In the authors' experience, the most preventable anticoagulant errors occur at transitions: the initial high-dose phase of apixaban and rivaroxaban, the parenteral lead-in for dabigatran and edoxaban, VKA overlap, duplication with residual heparin and prescriptions that do not cover the initiation phase. We therefore propose a minimum discharge bundle ( Table 8 ) that specifies the drug, dose and date of any dose change, the provisional duration and provoking context, bleeding mitigation, warning signs and a named clinician responsible for follow-up. The bundle operationalizes the AHA/ACC recommendations for clinical contact within the first week after discharge (Class 1), a visit at or before three months to decide on anticoagulation duration (Class 1), and systematic enquiry about PE-related symptoms and functional limitation at every visit for at least one year (Class 1) ( 9 ), as well as the ESC recommendation for routine re-evaluation three to six months after acute PE (Class I) ( 1 , 4 ).

Planned interruptions should be scheduled rather than improvised: heparin bridging during DOAC interruption is unnecessary and increases bleeding ( 70 ), and, in the authors' opinion, elective procedures should be deferred until the initial treatment phase has been completed whenever possible. 7.3. Communication and shared decision-making

Shared decision-making is essential when evidence supports more than one reasonable strategy: surveillance versus anticoagulation for isolated subsegmental PE, finite versus extended therapy, reduced-dose secondary prevention, elective CDI, and intervention for symptomatic CTEPD without resting pulmonary hypertension ( 4 , 9 ). The AHA/ACC guideline considers screening for anxiety and depression reasonable (Class 2a) ( 9 ). In the authors' opinion, explaining hemodynamic risk and the expected recovery trajectory is more informative for patients than anatomical terms such as “massive”. 8. Duration of anticoagulation and secondary prevention 8.1. The duration decision

All patients require at least three months of therapeutic anticoagulation; thereafter, the decision balances the risk of recurrence if treatment stops, the risk of bleeding if it continues, and patient preference ( 1 , 9 ). After a first unprovoked VTE, the cumulative risk of recurrence after stopping anticoagulation is approximately 10% at one year, 16% at two years, 25% at five years and 36% at ten years ( 15 ). A major transient provoking factor, such as major surgery, supports discontinuation after three months, whereas unprovoked PE, persistent risk factors, active cancer and recurrent VTE favor extended therapy ( 1 , 14 , 26 , 71 ). The AHA/ACC guideline recommends continuing anticoagulation—with reduced-dose apixaban or rivaroxaban as an option—after the initial three months unless the PE was a first event strongly provoked by a transient risk factor (Class 1) ( 9 ).

Reduced-dose DOACs combine efficacy with a favorable bleeding profile. In AMPLIFY-EXT, recurrent VTE or VTE-related death occurred in 8.8% with placebo versus 1.7% with apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily, with similar major bleeding ( 72 ); in EINSTEIN CHOICE, recurrence was 1.2% with rivaroxaban 10 mg versus 4.4% with aspirin ( 73 ). In RENOVE, which enrolled patients at high risk of recurrence, reduced-dose DOACs were non-inferior to full-dose DOACs for recurrent VTE (2.2% vs. 1.8%) and reduced clinically relevant bleeding (9.9% vs. 15.2%; hazard ratio 0.61) ( 74 ). In API-CAT, reduced-dose apixaban was non-inferior to full-dose apixaban for extended treatment of cancer-associated VTE (recurrence 2.1% vs. 2.8%), with less clinically relevant bleeding (12.1% vs. 15.6%) ( 75 ).

8.2. Dynamic reassessment of bleeding risk Bleeding risk is dynamic: age, kidney function, anemia, antiplatelet or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug use, uncontrolled hypertension, alcohol, falls and prior bleeding should be reviewed at each visit and modified where possible ( 1 , 4 ). In the authors' opinion, neither a previous PE nor a bleeding score should replace shared decision-making, and in older adults falls rarely justify withholding anticoagulation in isolation. 8.3. Special populations

In cancer-associated PE, thrombotic and bleeding risks vary with tumor site, mucosal involvement, anticancer therapy, thrombocytopenia and prognosis, and anticoagulation generally continues while cancer is active ( 24 ). Thrombocytopenia requires a graded strategy; full-dose anticoagulation is usually continued above 50 × 10⁹/L, whereas dose reduction, platelet support or temporary interruption are considered below this threshold depending on clot burden and time from the acute event ( 76 ). After estrogen-associated PE, estrogen-containing contraception is usually replaced by progestin-only or nonhormonal methods before anticoagulation ends; in an analysis of the EINSTEIN trials, continuing hormonal therapy during anticoagulation was not associated with an excess of recurrent VTE, whereas abnormal uterine bleeding was more frequent with rivaroxaban than with enoxaparin/VKA ( 77 ). Pregnancy-associated PE is treated with LMWH for at least six weeks postpartum and for a minimum total duration of three months, and future pregnancies require a prophylaxis plan ( 1 , 22 ). In severe or rapidly changing renal dysfunction, UFH may offer controllability, and DOAC selection must reflect drug clearance ( 1 ).

8.4. Suspected recurrence during anticoagulation Suspected recurrence requires objective confirmation and comparison with previous imaging, because residual abnormalities may persist ( 1 , 4 ). The evaluation should establish the drug and dose, adherence, interruptions, malabsorption, renal and hepatic function and interacting medication; when recurrence is confirmed despite verified exposure, cancer, antiphospholipid syndrome and heparin-induced thrombocytopenia should be considered, and a temporary switch to LMWH is commonly used (authors' opinion). 9. Post-PE syndrome, CTEPD and CTEPH 9.1. Definitions and hemodynamic thresholds

The post-pulmonary embolism (post-PE) syndrome is an umbrella term for new or persistent dyspnea, exercise limitation or impaired quality of life after at least three months of adequate anticoagulation that is not explained by other conditions ( 4 , 5 ). It comprises distinct phenotypes ( Table 9 ): symptoms without demonstrable cardiopulmonary impairment, frequently related to deconditioning or dysfunctional breathing; post-PE cardiac impairment with persistent RV dysfunction; CTEPD without pulmonary hypertension; and CTEPH ( 4 ). According to the 2022 ESC/ERS guidelines, pulmonary hypertension is defined at right-heart catheterization by a mean pulmonary arterial pressure (mPAP) > 20 mmHg, and pre-capillary pulmonary hypertension additionally requires a pulmonary arterial wedge pressure (PAWP) ≤ 15 mmHg and a PVR >2 Wood units (WU); exercise pulmonary hypertension is defined by an mPAP/cardiac output slope >3 mmHg/L/min between rest and exercise ( 10 ). CTEPH is pre-capillary pulmonary hypertension with mismatched perfusion defects and imaging signs of chronic thromboembolic obstruction after at least three months of effective anticoagulation ( 8 , 10 ). CTEPD is the broader term for symptomatic patients with these perfusion defects and chronic thromboembolic changes, with or without pulmonary hypertension at rest ( 8 , 10 ).
9.2. Frequency and the effect of acute reperfusion

Persistent limitation is common. In the prospective ELOPE cohort, 46.6% of patients had a peak oxygen uptake below 80% of predicted one year after PE ( 6 ). In FOCUS, the two-year cumulative incidence of post-PE impairment was 16.0% and that of CTEPH 2.3%; post-PE impairment identified 15 of the 16 patients eventually diagnosed with CTEPH ( 7 ). A meta-analysis estimated the incidence of CTEPH at 0.56% in all-comers, 3.2% in survivors and 2.8% in survivors without major comorbidities ( 78 ), consistent with earlier prospective cohorts reporting 1.5% and 3.8% at two years ( 79 , 80 ). Reperfusion has not been shown to prevent chronic sequelae: in the three-year follow-up of PEITHO, tenecteplase did not reduce CTEPH (2.1% vs. 3.2%), persistent dyspnea or functional limitation (36.0% vs. 30.1%), or residual pulmonary hypertension and RV dysfunction on echocardiography ( 48 ). Whether CDI modifies long-term outcomes is unknown, and the long-term data of HI-PEITHO and PE-TRACT are awaited ( 31 ).

9.3. Structured follow-up and screening algorithms A visit at approximately three months is the clinical anchor of follow-up ( 1 , 4 , 9 ). The Post-VTE Functional Status (PVFS) scale and the disease-specific Pulmonary Embolism Quality of Life (PEmb-QoL) questionnaire allow standardized and serial assessment ( 81 , 82 ). Routine imaging of asymptomatic patients and screening for CTEPH in asymptomatic survivors are not recommended (ESC Class III) ( 1 ), whereas symptomatic patients with mismatched perfusion defects beyond three months should be referred to a pulmonary hypertension/CTEPH center (ESC Class I) ( 1 ).

The ESC position paper proposes echocardiography for patients with persistent dyspnea, functional limitation or CTEPH risk factors, followed by V/Q scintigraphy and referral when pulmonary hypertension is probable ( 4 ). In the InShape II management study (424 patients), an algorithm combining the CTEPH prediction score with electrocardiography and N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) excluded CTEPH without echocardiography in 81% of patients, with a failure rate of 0.29% during two years, and identified 10 of the 13 CTEPH cases within four months ( 83 ). In InShape IV, adding a dedicated reading of the index CTPA for signs of chronic thromboembolism reduced the failure rate to 0%, with 20%–24% of patients requiring echocardiography ( 84 ), underlining the value of handing forward acute-phase imaging findings. A recent Delphi study among 39 European experts reached consensus that the three-month visit should assess the full spectrum of sequelae (CTEPH, CTEPD and post-PE syndrome) using patient-reported outcomes, that CPET is useful in persistent dyspnea, that right-heart catheterization belongs in specialized centers, that patients with persistent dyspnea need extended follow-up even after CTEPH and CTEPD are excluded, and that a single uniform protocol is preferable ( 85 , 86 ). Our pathway integrating these elements is shown in Figure 2 ; its screening components rest on prospective management studies, whereas visit timing and multidisciplinary organization rest on expert consensus ( 4 , 85 ).

9.4. Diagnostic tools for persistent symptoms

Transthoracic echocardiography is the usual first cardiac test when pulmonary hypertension or persistent RV dysfunction is suspected, but a low-probability echocardiogram does not end the investigation when symptoms are substantial ( 4 , 10 ). V/Q scintigraphy is the preferred screening test for chronic thromboembolic obstruction: in a referral cohort, its sensitivity for CTEPH was 96%–97%, compared with 51% for CTPA at the time ( 87 ), and a normal perfusion scan makes CTEPH very unlikely ( 10 ). CTPA characterizes chronic thromboembolic lesions, but subtle disease is easily missed outside expert centers ( 8 ). Cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET) can distinguish deconditioning, ventilatory inefficiency, circulatory limitation, dysfunctional breathing and pulmonary vascular physiology; low end-tidal carbon dioxide and a high ventilatory equivalent for carbon dioxide suggest pulmonary vascular limitation ( 4 , 10 ). Right-heart catheterization is required to confirm pulmonary hypertension and define hemodynamics before treatment ( 10 ).

The differential diagnosis of persistent dyspnea includes heart failure, ischemic and valvular disease, arrhythmia, chronic lung disease, anemia or iron deficiency, thyroid disease, obesity, sleep-disordered breathing, deconditioning, dysfunctional breathing and anxiety ( 4 ). Repeating CTPA without a specific hypothesis often detects residual material that does not establish causality; a staged evaluation (history, examination, electrocardiography, blood count, NT-proBNP and echocardiography, followed by targeted pulmonary function tests, V/Q scintigraphy or CPET) is more informative, and abrupt new breathlessness should be investigated for recurrence with comparison to baseline imaging ( 1 , 4 ).
9.5. Rehabilitation

Mechanisms often coexist, and treating residual perfusion defects while ignoring deconditioning will not restore function. The evidence for rehabilitation consists of small randomized trials with heterogeneous populations and inconsistent results. Early-initiation exercise training was safe and improved fitness in a pilot randomized trial ( 88 ), and structured inpatient rehabilitation was feasible and safe ( 89 ). In a randomized trial of 140 unselected patients, a physiotherapist-guided home-based program did not significantly improve physical capacity compared with usual care ( 90 ), whereas in a randomized trial of 211 patients with persistent dyspnea 6–72 months after PE, eight weeks of supervised exercise training improved disease-specific quality of life and incremental shuttle walk distance ( 91 ). Rehabilitation should therefore be targeted to symptomatic patients after exclusion of CTEPH rather than offered indiscriminately. The AHA/ACC guideline considers early ambulation rather than bed rest reasonable (Class 2a) ( 9 ); in the authors' opinion, addressing fear of recurrence is an integral part of recovery.
9.6. Treatment of CTEPH and CTEPD

Suspected CTEPH should be evaluated by a multidisciplinary CTEPH team before any patient is declared inoperable ( 8 , 10 ). Pulmonary endarterectomy is the potentially curative treatment of choice for operable disease (ESC/ERS Class I); in an international prospective registry, three-year survival was 89% in operated and 70% in non-operated patients ( 92 ), and in-hospital mortality has fallen to approximately 2% at highly experienced centers ( 93 ). Balloon pulmonary angioplasty (BPA) is recommended for technically inoperable disease or residual pulmonary hypertension after surgery (Class I) ( 10 ). In the RACE trial, BPA reduced PVR by approximately 60% versus 32% with riociguat at 26 weeks, at the cost of more procedure-related serious adverse events ( 94 ), and the MR BPA trial similarly showed greater hemodynamic improvement with BPA than with riociguat ( 95 ). Both trials support a sequential approach in which medical therapy precedes BPA in selected patients ( 10 , 94 ).

Riociguat is recommended for inoperable or persistent/recurrent CTEPH (Class I); in CHEST-1, it improved six-minute walk distance by 46 m versus placebo, and PVR decreased by 226 dyn·s·cm⁻⁵ with riociguat versus an increase of 23 dyn·s·cm⁻⁵ with placebo ( 96 ). Subcutaneous treprostinil improved six-minute walk distance in severe non-operable CTEPH in the CTREPH trial (Class IIb) ( 97 ). Macitentan improved PVR in the phase 2 MERIT-1 trial, with sustained effects in its open-label extension ( 98 ), but the phase 3 MACiTEPH trial of macitentan 75 mg was stopped for futility on its primary endpoint of six-minute walk distance ( 99 ); its role therefore remains limited. Lifelong anticoagulation is recommended in CTEPH, with VKAs preferred in antiphospholipid syndrome ( 10 ). In symptomatic CTEPD without resting pulmonary hypertension, pulmonary endarterectomy improved symptoms and exercise capacity in selected patients at an experienced center ( 100 ), but this evidence is limited to single-center observational series, so intervention requires careful confirmation that obstruction is causally important and should be decided in expert centers ( 8 , 10 ).
10. Implementation in real-world clinical systems 10.1. From PERT activation to longitudinal care

A mature PE program connects acute and outpatient care: the acute team records diagnostic certainty, provoking factors, RV and biomarker findings, treatment, complications, the intended anticoagulant course and follow-up triggers, and the outpatient team receives this information directly ( 4 , 101 ). Standardized referral matters after advanced reperfusion too, because reperfusion has not been shown to prevent chronic sequelae ( 48 ). The AHA/ACC guideline considers follow-up in a specialized PE clinic reasonable for complex patients (Class 2a) ( 9 ). In the authors' opinion, a tiered model can return uncomplicated low-risk patients to primary or general care with a clear protocol, while recurrent, cancer-associated, pregnancy-associated, bleeding-prone, reperfused or persistently symptomatic patients receive specialist review.
10.2. Episode-wide quality indicators

We propose quality indicators covering the complete episode of care [authors' proposal, derived from guideline recommendations ( 1 , 4 , 9 )]: (i) appropriate probability-based diagnosis; (ii) time to anticoagulation; (iii) documented risk category, including lactate in AHA/ACC categories C–E; (iv) correct discharge dose and transition schedule; (v) outpatient-eligibility assessment in low-risk patients; (vi) a documented provisional duration; (vii) completion of contact within one week; (viii) completion of a three-month review with standardized functional assessment (for example, PVFS); (ix) bleeding and recurrence at three and twelve months; (x) time from persistent symptoms to V/Q scintigraphy; and (xi) time to expert CTEPH referral. Patient-reported experience should be included, and the indicators require validation.
11. Critical appraisal, evidence gaps and research priorities

The evidence underpinning the recommendations discussed in this review is heterogeneous, and recommendations supported by randomized trials, prospective cohorts, device registries and expert consensus should not be presented with equivalent certainty. Table 10 therefore summarizes, for each key recommendation, the type of evidence available and the resulting level of certainty. Evidence for anticoagulation is robust, but important contemporary questions rest on weaker foundations. Until recently, CDI studies prioritized the RV/LV ratio at 24–48 h, enrolled selected patients and lacked randomized controls; observational comparisons are vulnerable to confounding by indication because the sickest patients are more likely to receive advanced treatment ( 11 , 58 ). HI-PEITHO has narrowed but not closed this gap, because its benefit was confined to early physiological deterioration in a highly selected population ( 31 ). No randomized trial has compared MT with local thrombolysis in high-risk PE or tested any CDI against anticoagulation for long-term functional outcomes.

Long-term research is limited by inconsistent, overlapping definitions of post-PE syndrome, post-PE impairment, CTEPD and post-PE cardiac impairment, so prevalence depends on the definition used and on which patients return for assessment ( 5 , 7 , 8 ). Future trials need core outcomes encompassing survival, recurrence, major bleeding, hemodynamic deterioration, functional recovery, quality of life and diagnostic delay ( 4 ). Further priorities include validated dynamic risk models that do not multiply categories without changing treatment, phenotype-targeted rehabilitation trials, evaluation of whether systematic follow-up clinics improve time to CTEPH diagnosis and cost-effectiveness ( 102 ), and the inclusion of women, pregnant patients, older and frail adults, patients with cancer or renal dysfunction, and socioeconomically disadvantaged groups in PE trials ( Table 11 ).

Conclusions

PE care should be designed as one longitudinal episode ( Figure 1 ). The ESC and AHA/ACC frameworks differ in terminology but converge on the principles that hemodynamics defines urgency, that RV dysfunction, myocardial injury, lactate and clinical trajectory refine prognosis in normotensive patients, and that anticoagulation—preferably with a DOAC—is the foundation of treatment. Systemic thrombolysis remains reserved for high-risk (category E) PE. HI-PEITHO provides the first randomized evidence that CDI reduces early decompensation in carefully selected intermediate-high-risk patients, but survival and long-term functional benefits remain unproven, and MT is the preferred CDI when fibrinolysis is absolutely contraindicated. The discharge process must convert a successful acute intervention into a safe recovery plan, with early contact and a structured three-month review. Persistent symptoms warrant phenotype-directed evaluation rather than automatic repeat CTPA, with V/Q scintigraphy as the screening test for chronic thromboembolic disease, hemodynamic confirmation using the 2022 thresholds and early referral to an expert center, where pulmonary endarterectomy, BPA and medical therapy can be combined.

Over the past decades, pulmonary embolism (PE) remains a leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide. Management has shifted from broad protocols to more precise strategies. In clinical practice, physicians continue to search for validated diagnostic algorithms that support reliable decision making. Personalized treatment is increasingly replacing the traditional model in which all patients nearly receive the same care. In 2025, many high quality studies pushed the field closer to this goal. The following sections summarize the major developments in pulmonary embolism research this year ( Figure 1 ). Figure 1. Open in a new tab

Key advances in pulmonary embolism (PE) management across prediction, treatment and novel therapies. Selected visual elements were adapted from the cited article and from publicly available resources on Drugs.com ( https://www.drugs.com/cg/mechanical-thrombectomy.html ). Streamlined diagnosis and precision prognostics

Diagnostic strategies for PE shifted towards simplification and higher precision. The modified D-dimer strategy (MODS) validated a streamlined approach where physicians raised a single question: “Is PE the most likely diagnosis?” If it is “no,” then a D-dimer below 1000 ng/mL will rule out PE without imaging, and if it is “yes,” an age-adjusted threshold should be considered. This method reduced CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA) use by 19% while maintaining a 0.00% failure rate. [ 1 ] However, experts caution that the safety of this strategy relies heavily on the clinicians’ experience. Simultaneously, risk stratification has advanced from broad categories to precise calculation. The newly validated “eStiMaTe” Multimarker Calculator integrates sPESI, troponin, BNP, and DVT status. In a cohort of over 60,000 patients, it predicted 30-day mortality with superior accuracy compared to the traditional ESC model (C-statistic 0.79 vs . 0.56). [ 2 ] Despite these advances, clinicians still face uncertainty when radiology reports are ambiguous, and many initiate anticoagulation unnecessarily to act cautiously. Furthermore, precision in biomarker assessment has also been refined. An analysis of the China pUlmonary Thromboembolism REgistry Study (CURES) involving 4105 patients highlighted the necessity of age-adjusted thresholds for natriuretic peptides to detect right ventricular dysfunction (RVD). The study established that optimal NT-proBNP cut-offs increase with age (< 55 years: 356 pg/mL; 55–69 years: 526 pg/mL; ≥ 70 years: 647 pg/mL), offering improved sensitivity for identifying high-risk patients compared to a single universal threshold. For risk assessment, a CURES registry analysis identified the RIETE score as the optimal predictor for major bleeding (AUC 0.70). This stratification proved clinically actionable, as low-risk patients treated initially with direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) experienced significantly fewer 14-day adverse outcomes than those receiving low molecular weight heparin (HR 0.13).

Acute management: the interventional era The STORM-PE trial was the first RCT comparing computer assisted vacuum thrombectomy (CAVT) plus anticoagulation versus anticoagulation alone in intermediate-high risk PE. CAVT reduced the RV/LV ratio by 0.52 at 48 h, more than double the reduction in the control group, without increasing major adverse events at 7 d. [ 3 ]

Anticoagulation remains the cornerstone for hemodynamically stable patients, and escalation should be individualized. [ 4 ] A retrospective study found that patients with lower cardiac index and marked RV dysfunction derived the greatest benefit from mechanical thrombectomy. [ 5 ] Routine reperfusion for all intermediate-risk patients is not justified. Multidisciplinary evaluation should be prioritized for those with impending decompensation, heavy central clot burden, or unfavorable hemodynamic profiles.

For high-risk patients with shock or cardiac arrest, systemic thrombolysis remains the first-line reperfusion strategy in most emergency settings, [ 6 ] particularly when immediate catheter-based or surgical options are not available. However, recent studies suggest that management should be further individualized in patients with profound hemodynamic collapse or failed initial reperfusion. A target trial emulation of nearly 1000 patients revealed that venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) alone resulted in the highest in-hospital mortality of 57%, whereas combination of VA-ECMO with surgical thrombectomy was associated with the best survival outcomes, reducing mortality to 34%. [ 7 ] In parallel, emerging comparative data indicate that surgical pulmonary embolectomy may provide favorable short-term outcomes compared with thrombolysis in selected patients with high-risk PE. [ 8 ] Together, these findings support the view that ECMO serves best as a bridge to definitive reperfusion rather than a standalone treatment, and that reperfusion strategies for high-risk PE should be selected according to bleeding risk, treatment response, and local expertise.

Extended anticoagulation strategies Extended anticoagulation strategies now diverge based on cancer status. The API-CAT trial studied patients with active cancer who completed 6 months of treatment. Comparing full-dose versus reduced-dose apixaban, the reduced-dose proved non-inferior for preventing recurrence while offering superior safety by significantly lowering clinically-relevant-bleeding. This establishes dose reduction as the new standard for stable cancer patients. [ 9 ]

In contrast, the RENOVE trial examined non cancer patients with unprovoked VTE or persistent risk factors. Comparing full-dose direct oral versus reduced DOACs, the reduced-dose failed to meet statistical non-inferiority for recurrence risk. Consequently, non-cancer patients at high-risk of recurrence should generally maintain full-dose anticoagulation for maximum protection. [ 10 ] PE management in special populations

Obesity presents a clinical paradox where patients face higher PE risk yet often exhibit lower mortality than normal weight individuals. Diagnosis proves difficult due to imaging artifacts and reduced D-dimer specificity. Management requires dosing low molecular weight heparins (LMWH) by actual body weight and exercising caution with DOACs in cases of severe obesity. In pregnancy, diagnostic pathways must balance maternal benefit against fetal radiation exposure. LMWH remains the preferred anticoagulant; thrombolysis or interventional reperfusion should be reserved for hemodynamic collapse or life-threatening PE. [ 11 ]

In older adults, PE management is complicated by frailty, renal dysfunction, polypharmacy, and elevated risks of both thrombosis and bleeding. Clinical decisions should integrate comorbidity burden, functional status, and drug interaction risk rather than chronological age alone. [ 12 ]

Patients at high bleeding risk represent another important subgroup in whom treatment intensity must be individualized. In these patients, the choice and duration of anticoagulation, and the decision to pursue catheter-based or surgical reperfusion, should be guided by a careful balance between the risk of hemorrhage and the expected benefit of preventing hemodynamic deterioration or recurrence. Pediatric PE displays a bimodal incidence peak in infants under one year and adolescents aged 15 to 19 years old. Mortality is extremely high in children aged 0 to 9 with high-risk features, reaching 25.3%, which underscores the need for aggressive monitoring. [ 13 ] Additionally, nationwide data tracked the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, finding a 52% incidence surge in 2021 driven by males largely. Fortunately, rates began returning to pre-pandemic levels by 2022. [ 14 ]
New directions in thrombosis and anticoagulation therapy

Innovative basic science is introducing advanced therapeutic platforms. A study introduced a bismuth-based nanoplatform (PBTH) for integrated diagnosis and treatment. This “theranostic” tool targets P-selectin on activated endothelial cells and is activated by hypoxia to emit NIR-II fluorescence for precise thrombus visualization. It simultaneously releases hydrogen sulfide and drugs (TNK/HCQ) to dissolve clots and reduce inflammation. [ 15 ] New anticoagulant agents targeting Factor XI are being developed to reduce thrombosis without increasing bleeding. Two phase II trials compared the Factor XI antibodies REGN9933 and REGN7508 against enoxaparin in patients undergoing knee surgery. REGN7508 proved superior to enoxaparin for preventing VTE. Importantly, neither antibody increased bleeding risk compared to enoxaparin. This confirms Factor XI as a promising target for safer anticoagulation beyond Factor Xa inhibitor. [ 16 ]

Conclusion 2025 marks a new era of precision medicine for PE, driven by smarter diagnostics and advanced therapy. These developments are expected to influence future clinical guidelines and gradually reshape the standard of care. Acknowledgements None. Funding Statement None. Footnotes Author Contributions Z. PMC Copyright notice PMCID: PMC13737865 PMID: 42989369 Abstract Background In patients with acute pulmonary embolism (PE), hypoxia may increase pulmonary vascular resistance and worsen right ventricular dysfunction (RVD), which is a key prognostic factor. However, associations between hypoxia, RVD and clinical outcomes have not been well described. Aim To describe associations between hypoxia, RVD and clinical outcomes in patients with PE. Methods

We performed a retrospective, single-center cohort study of patients treated by the Massachusetts General Hospital Pulmonary Embolism Response Team (PERT) from 10/2012 to 08/2021. Inclusion criteria included confirmed PE, recorded oxygen saturation prior to PERT activation, and echocardiogram within three days of PERT activation. Patients were categorized into four subgroups based on (1) hypoxia status (SaO₂ below vs. above 95%) and, (2) oxygen support (below vs. above 3 L/min). Our primary outcome was the presence of RVD on echocardiogram. Our secondary outcome was clinical deterioration within 7 days. Results

We included 894 PE patients. The mean age was 61 (± 16 SD), 614/894 (69%) were hypoxic, and 624/894 (70%) had RVD on echocardiogram. Overall, hypoxic patients were more likely to have RVD than non-hypoxic patients (467/614 [76%] vs. 157/280 [56%], p < 0.0001). On subgroup analysis, RVD prevalence was highest in the “hypoxic with oxygen support ≥3L” group ( n = 216/266, 81%) followed by the “not hypoxic with oxygen support ≥3L” group 53/70 (76%); 198/278 (71%) in the “hypoxic with oxygen support <3L” and 157/280 (56%) in the “not hypoxic with oxygen support <3L” groups. Clinical deterioration occurred in 199/894 (22%) patients and was more common in hypoxic patients than non-hypoxic patients (157/614 [26%] vs. 42/280 [15%], p < 0.0001), and most common in the “hypoxic with oxygen support ≥3L” subgroup 88/266 (33%).

Conclusions Hypoxia is associated with RVD and clinical deterioration in patients with PE. More research is needed to understand the risk associated with hypoxia and the physiology of supplemental oxygen support in PE. Clinical trial number Not applicable. Keywords: Clinical outcomes, Echocardiography, Risk stratification, Prognosis of PE, Venous thromboembolism, Oxygen, Pulmonary vasoconstriction Introduction

Pulmonary embolism (PE) is one of the leading causes of cardiovascular mortality in the United States [ 1 , 3 ]. Severe PE manifests as both hemodynamic and respiratory compromise. The combination of mechanical obstruction and pulmonary vasoconstriction, which is worsened by hypoxia, increases pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR). The resulting right ventricular (RV) pressure overload leads to increased RV workload and reduced RV coronary perfusion resulting in RV oxygen demand/supply mismatch and RV myocardial ischemia. This sequence may manifest as right ventricular dysfunction (RVD), which is directly linked to mortality and is considered the primary cause of death in severe PE. Accordingly, both hypoxia and RVD play significant roles in the vicious cycle of acute PE pathophysiology [ 1 , 4 , 5 ].

Hypoxia in patients with PE represents not only a risk factor but also a potential therapeutic target. A recent study of a porcine model of PE showed that supplemental oxygen reduced PVR and improved RV function [ 6 ]. Similar effects were observed in a clinical trial of supplemental oxygen in patients with acute PE [ 7 ]. There is a lack of studies linking hypoxia with RVD and outcomes, especially considering subgroups based on O 2 saturation and O 2 supplementation, which reflect the realities of clinical practice in which most hypoxic PE patients are treated with supplemental oxygen.

In this study, we aimed to investigate the associations between hypoxia, RVD, and clinical deterioration in patients with acute PE. We hypothesized that hypoxia or the need for supplemental oxygen would be associated with more frequent RVD and worse clinical outcomes. Methods Study design and data acquisition

We performed a retrospective, single-center cohort study. We enrolled all patients for whom the Massachusetts General Hospital (MGH) pulmonary embolism response team (PERT) was activated from October 2012 to August 2021. MGH is an urban, academic tertiary care center. Since its inception in 2012, the PERT at MGH has followed a multidisciplinary approach to the treatment of PE [ 8 ]. The goal of the PERT is to quickly enlist the assistance of multiple specialists to assess a patient with PE, mobilize resources, and facilitate advanced treatment when needed [ 9 ]. PERT is activated at the treating physician’s discretion not dictated by any protocol. Data describing each patient evaluated by the MGH PERT is entered in a web-based registry (REDCap™, www.projectredcap.org ) [ 10 ]. The MGH PERT data registry captures information related to patient demographics, clinical presentation, diagnostic procedures, treatment, and outcomes across several follow-up timepoints. The registry is approved by the MassGeneralBrigham IRB (protocol number 2016P000179) under a waiver of informed consent as a retrospective database.

Inclusion and exclusion criteria We included patients with Computed Tomography Pulmonary Angiography (CTPA)-confirmed PE, a recorded oxygen saturation from pulse oximetry at the time of PERT activation, and an echocardiogram performed within three days of PERT activation. We excluded patients who underwent advanced interventions such as systemic thrombolysis, catheter-based intervention, surgical embolectomy, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) before the echocardiogram was performed as these interventions could influence the presence of RVD on echocardiogram. Definitions of hypoxia, RVD and outcomes

We defined hypoxia based on the lowest oxygen saturation (SaO 2 ) and the maximal amount of oxygen support the patient required during the 12 h prior to PERT activation. Significant oxygen supplementation was defined as: 3L or more per minute by nasal cannula, use of a nonrebreather mask, continuous or biphasic positive pressure ventilation (CPAP or BIPAP), or mechanical ventilation. Non-hypoxic patients had an SaO 2 ≧95% and oxygen supplementation below 3L per minute. In a 2 × 2 manner, we further divided the patients into four subgroups: (1) SaO 2 <95% with supplemental oxygen; (2) SaO 2 <95% without supplemental oxygen; (3) SaO 2 ≧95% with supplemental oxygen; and (4) SaO 2 ≧95% without supplemental oxygen. Patients were defined as “hypoxic” if they belonged to groups 1, 2 or 3.

The primary outcome was the presence of RVD on echocardiogram performed within the first 3 days following PERT activation. RVD was defined as RV dilatation, RV free wall hypokinesis, septal bowing, or right ventricular systolic pressure (RVSP) > 36 mmHg [ 11 ]. Our secondary outcome was a 7-day composite outcome of clinical deterioration defined as all-cause mortality, treatment with systemic intravenous (IV) thrombolysis, a catheter-based intervention (thrombolysis or thromboembolectomy), surgical thromboembolectomy, or extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO), or hypotension requiring vasopressors. Statistical analysis

Categorical variables are presented as frequencies with percentages and continuous variables with standard deviations. We compared characteristics of hypoxic and non-hypoxic patients using Fisher’s exact and T-tests for categorical and continuous variables, respectively, to identify potential confounders to include in multivariable models. We compared outcomes between patient subgroups defined by hypoxia and/or oxygen support using Fisher’s exact test and logistic regression. We performed multivariable logistic regression adjusting for age, coronary artery disease (CAD), chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), family history of deep vein thrombosis/pulmonary embolism (DVT/PE), and smoking status. Additionally, we stratified patients into subgroups based on presence vs. absence of hypoxia and RVD to assess the association between these factors and clinical deterioration. SAS version 9.4 was used for all analyses. The significance level for statistical tests was set at 0.05 without adjustment for multiple comparisons due to the exploratory nature of the analyses.
Results

A total of 1551 patients were enrolled in the MGH PERT data registry, of whom 894 (58%) patients met our inclusion criteria (Fig. 1 ). The mean age was 61 (± 16) years. The median time from PERT activation to TTE was 15.6 h (IQR 2.0–46.0). Of the 657 patients we excluded from the study, 274 (42%) had no imaging-confirmed PE, 213 (32%) did not have a recorded echocardiogram within three days of PERT activation, 72 (12%) received advanced interventions prior to the echocardiogram and 90 (14%) met criteria for clinical deterioration before PERT activation. Of 894 patients included in the study, 614 (69%) were hypoxic and 199 (22%) had clinical deterioration. Patient characteristics are in Table 1 .

There were 624/894 (70%) patients who had RVD on echocardiogram of which 436 (70%) had RV dilatation, 392 (63%) had RV free wall hypokinesis, 295 (47%) had septal bowing, and 379 (61%) had RVSP > 36 mmHg. Table 2 shows that the prevalence of RVD was significantly higher in hypoxic patients than in non-hypoxic patients ( n = 467 [76%] vs. n = 157 [56%], p < 0.0001; unadjusted odds ratio (OR) 2.49 [95% CI 1.84–3.36]). On multivariate analysis, hypoxia remained associated with RVD, with odds of RVD 2.49 times higher in hypoxic patients compared to non-hypoxic patients (OR 2.49 [95% CI 1.83–3.41], p < 0.0001) The remaining co-variates are presented in Supplementary Table 1 with significant associations for age and COPD. Comparisons of individual subgroups of hypoxia are available in Supplementary Table 2 . Within the subgroups of hypoxia, RVD was most prevalent ( n = 216, 81%) in group 1 (SaO 2 <95% and oxygen support ≥3L). The prevalence of RVD was second highest in group 3 (SaO₂ ≥95% with oxygen support ≥3L) ( n = 53, 76%) and was followed by group 2 (SaO₂ <95% with O₂ support <3L) ( n = 198, 71%). The lowest prevalence of RVD was observed in group 4 (SaO₂ ≥95% with O₂ support <3L) ( n = 157, 56%). Hypoxia remained associated with each of the four components encompassing RVD (see Supplementary Table 3 ).

Discussion

Among patients with acute PE, we found hypoxia to be independently associated with both RVD and clinical deterioration. When patients present with hypoxia, standard clinical practice requires oxygen supplementation, so it is challenging to independently assess the effect of hypoxia and supplemental oxygen use. We therefore used a definition that both combines and separates oxygen saturation and oxygen supplementation. Our findings show that hypoxia despite oxygen supplementation is most strongly associated with RVD and clinical deterioration. Hypoxia in acute pulmonary embolism

Acute PE causes ventilation-perfusion mismatch and hypoxia due to which triggers hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction leading to an increase in RV afterload. The normal RV is very susceptible to acute pressure overload, which can result in RV dilation which increase wall tension and myocardial work and oxygen demand. However, both the increased RV pressure and wall tension and a low systemic and coronary blood pressure compromises RV myocardial perfusion and thereby oxygen supply. Hypoxemia worsens the supply. Collectively, the RV will experience a oxygen supply-demand mismatch causing RV ischemia, impaired systolic function, and ultimately RV failure which is cause of death in acute PE [ 12 , 13 ].

Oxygen supplementation may modulate this pathophysiology by counteracting some of the hemodynamic consequences of hypoxia. We have previously demonstrated that supplemental oxygen is associated with a reduced pulmonary vascular resistance and improved RV function in an animal model of acute PE [ 6 ]. If oxygen have similar effects in human PE remain unknown, but clinical data have shown promising effects as well and further studies are pending [ 7 , 14 , 15 ]. Oxygen is known to reduce pulmonary vascular resistance and pulmonary artery pressure in human related conditions such as pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) and chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) [ 14 , 16 – 18 ]. emphasizing the potential of supplemental oxygen in human PE.

Association between hypoxia and right ventricular function and outcome In this study, we found hypoxia associated with both RVD and clinical deterioration. This confirms previous findings by Subramanian et al. who reported hypoxia to be associated with of RVD and 30-day mortality [ 5 ]. Grifoni et al. also demonstrated that PE patients with RVD were more likely to be hypoxic [ 10 ].

Hypoxia is not included in all PE risk stratification models, nor is routine oxygen supplementation recommended for patients with SaO₂ > 90% [ 1 ]. The simplified Pulmonary Embolism Severity Index (sPESI) does include hypoxia < 90% as an independent risk factor associated with 30-day mortality in patients with PE [ 19 , 23 ]. However, other scores, as the Bova score, do not include hypoxia [ 19 , 21 , 24 ] We chose a stricter 95% cut-off and still found a robust association between hypoxia and adverse outcomes, and our results highlight the potential role of hypoxia in PE risk stratification. Contrary to the potential therapeutic effects of oxygen supplementation, our study shows that patients receiving oxygen were more likely to have RVD and experience clinical deterioration. However, this likely reflects confounding by indication, as the decision to provide supplemental oxygen often signifies more symptomatic PE.

We also found an association between hypoxia and clinical deterioration. This is comparable to prior studies of both intermediate-risk [ 12 , 25 ] and high-risk[ 5 , 24 ] acute PE. Our data confirm the well described association between RVD and clinical deterioration [ 26 , 27 ]. However, the present study adds the higher risk of clinical deterioration among patients with both RVD and hypoxia suggesting a synergistic interaction of these pathophysiological factors. Our results may aid clinical decision-making, since the data suggest that PE patients presenting with hypoxia, especially if not easily corrected by supplementary oxygen, are at higher risk of developing RVD and clinical deterioration. Clinicians could consider (persistent) hypoxia as a warning sign warranting closer observation, but such strategy needs to be confirmed in a prospective study.
Limitations

Our study has several limitations that warrant consideration. This study is a retrospective analysis of a prospective registry, so cannot establish causality. We also compared oxygen saturations and supplementation measured prior to PERT activation, though some echocardiographic data were not collected until after PERT activation. Furthermore, we did not have data on previous echocardiograms could therefore not distinguish between pre-existing RVD or RVD caused by the index PE. The presence and severity of hypoxia may have influenced clinicians determining the urgency of treatment and the need for advanced therapeutic interventions. Because we excluded patients who did not have echocardiograms prior to an advanced intervention, this could have introduced bias by excluding patients with low saturations from our analysis. However, that bias would most likely have driven our results towards the null, so we do not think this had a significant effect. Lastly, the study was conducted at a single center in Boston only including patients for whom PERT was activated, i.e. typically patients with central PE, high clot burden, RVD or other high-risk factors. This selection bias and limited generalizability affect any direct translation of our results to an overall PE population.

Conclusion Our study demonstrated an association between hypoxia, RVD, and clinical deterioration in patients with acute PE. This association was particularly pronounced in patients who were hypoxic despite oxygen support. These findings underscore the importance of further research into the management of hypoxia in PE patients.
